query: For high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, corrosion-related uses, and other applications requiring thermal stability, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their premelting and melting behavior and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing factor, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In HEA nanoparticles, the onset of premelting and overall melting behavior is governed primarily by surface composition heterogeneity: nanoparticles that undergo post‐synthesis thermal annealing develop surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements, which act as nucleation sites for melting at lower temperatures compared to homogenously composed nanoparticles.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA nanoparticles synthesized with homogeneous elemental distributions (e.g., via rapid thermal shock methods as in HEA-CoxMoy systems)
generation.intervention: A controlled post-synthesis thermal annealing treatment designed to induce surface segregation of the lower-melting-point elements
generation.conditions: Both sets of HEA nanoparticles (annealed vs. as-synthesized) should be tested under identical heating rates and environmental conditions (e.g., inert atmosphere) over a temperature range spanning below the expected premelting onset to beyond bulk melting temperatures
generation.structural_mediator: Surface compositional gradients—specifically the enrichment of lower-melting-point elements at the nanoparticle surfaces—mediating localized reduction in cohesive energy
generation.mechanism: Thermal annealing promotes diffusion of lower-melting-point elements to the surface, reducing local binding energy and thus facilitating premelting nucleation sites. This segregation decreases the effective melting temperature for the nanoparticles by locally weakening the metallic bonds at the surface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Annealed nanoparticles with segregated surfaces will exhibit premelting at lower temperatures (earlier onset of melting features observed in techniques such as in-situ TEM heating or DSC) compared to the homologously synthesized nanoparticles. The effect should be evidenced by a measurable reduction in melting onset and broader melting transition in the annealed samples.
generation.baseline: Homogeneously composed HEA nanoparticles with a uniform distribution of constituent elements, expected to display higher and sharper melting transitions
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for HEA nanoparticle systems where at least one component has a significantly lower melting point and sufficient atomic mobility exists during annealing to allow surface segregation. Extreme compositions or synthesis conditions that inherently promote segregation might fall outside this regime.
generation.uncertainty: While the predicted melting onset difference is anticipated to be significant, its magnitude depends on the specific elemental composition and annealing parameters; precise quantitative differences remain to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one set remains in the as-synthesized (homogeneous) state and the other set is subjected to controlled post-synthesis annealing to induce surface segregation. Using in-situ TEM heating experiments and differential scanning calorimetry under identical conditions, monitor the onset of premelting and complete melting transitions.
measurements: Temperature at which premelting begins (onset temperature)
Melting temperature (peak or complete melting point)
Surface composition mapping (via STEM-EDS) before and after annealing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed nanoparticles do not display a statistically significant decrease in the onset of melting temperature or a broader melting transition compared to the homogeneous nanoparticles, or if no clear differences in surface compositions are observed, then the hypothesis that surface segregation governs melting behavior would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High entropy oxide nanoparticles (HEO NPs) with multiple component elements possess improved stability and multiple uses for functional applications, including catalysis, data memory, and energy storage. However, the synthesis of homogenous HEO NPs containing five or more immiscible elements with a single-phase structure is still a great challenge due to the strict synthetic conditions. In particular, several synthesis methods of HEO NPs require extremely high temperatures. In this study, we demonstrate a low cost, facile, and effective method to synthesize three- to eight-element HEO nanoparticles by a combination of electrospinning and low-temperature ambient annealing. HEO NPs were generated by annealing nanofibers at 330 °C for 30 minutes under air conditions. The average size of the HEO nanoparticles was ∼30 nm and homogenous element distribution was obtained from post-electrospinning thermal decomposition. The synthesized HEO NPs exhibited magnetic properties with the highest saturation magnetization at 9.588 emu g−1 and the highest coercivity at 147.175 Oe for HEO NPs with four magnetic elements while integrating more nonmagnetic elements will suppress the magnetic response.

Bulk materials have very low dispersion, i.e., a low ratio of surface to bulk atoms. A large surface-to-bulk atom ratio is, however, vital for efficient catalysts. Nanoparticles possess such high dispersion. This generates a large interest in developing HEA nanoparticle synthesis methods. Many synthesis methods for HEA nanoparticles are high-energy shock methods such as Joule-heating, microwave heating, laser-ablation, and fast-bed pyrolysis. Recent studies propose that it is also possible to use low-temperature solution-based techniques to synthesize HEA nanoparticles or low-temperature reduction of solid precursors. Such methods open for fine-tuning both the composition and nanostructure of nanoparticles. For high-temperature synthesis approaches, entropy plays a role in stabilizing the multi-metallic phases, so that single-phase materials can be prepared. Thermal shock methods are also believed to freeze the material in a state of high entropy during controlled cool-down. The underlying mechanisms driving Cu and Pd segregation can be elucidated through Helmholtz free energy components F = U – TS of canonical ensembles, encompassing internal energy (U) and entropy (S). According to the cohesion theory, the cohesive energy trend among late transition and noble metals is mainly dictated by the d-band, approximated as where Wd represents the d-band width and Nd is the number of d-electrons. For Cu, with a fully occupied d-band (Nd = 10), its cohesive contribution is minimal, making metallic bonds with Cu energetically less favorable. Consequently, to minimize the system’s internal energy, Cu atoms tend to segregate onto the surface. Pd has only marginally higher cohesive and surface energies compared to Cu, which partially contributes to the surface segregation of Pd. Moreover, given the abundance of Pd in the HEA’s bulk composition (Pd0.25Cu0.20Pt0.20Ni0.22Co0.13 as targeted in our simulations), segregation to the surface occurs as the bulk strives for an equimolar distribution to maximize the configurational entropy, thereby rationalizing the segregation of Pd atoms at the HEA surface as observed in Monte Carlo simulations. cited_evidence.text: The CoMoFeNiCu HEA nanoparticles were synthesized by employing flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon supports, with the temperature going up to 2000–2300 K, the temperature ramping rate on the order of 105 K s−1 and the duration of shocks as short as ~55 ms (Fig. 2a–c). Under such conditions, the high temperature induced rapid thermal-decomposition of the precursors, forming small liquid droplets of multimetallic solutions. The subsequent rapid cooling enabled crystallization of these liquid droplets into uniform and homogeneous alloy nanoparticles without being subjected to aggregation/agglomeration, element segregation or phase separation. Five types of HEA nanoparticles with the general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 (x + y = 70) were prepared by using this method, in which the atomic ratio of Co/Mo was controlled to be 15/55, 25/45, 35/35, 45/25, and 55/15 by varying the loading of precursors, the overall loading of metals in each catalyst was controlled at 10 wt% during synthesis.
